turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Come through. I've just put him on the scales, today he's 3.51 kilograms. Birth weight in the book was 3.46, so he's up a touch.
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Oh that's a relief, I was sure he'd dropped off. The pram wheel squeaked the whole way from the car park, I nearly turned around.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, just logging in, this screen's crawling. What brings you in with him?
[SEG0004] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's gone yellow. Face and chest, proper yellow, not just a bit sallow from the light.
[SEG0005] person_4 (PATIENT): Ah.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yellow, right. How old is he?
[SEG0007] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ten days today. Vaginal birth, no drama, home on day two. My sister reckons he already looks like my husband, which is, um, generous.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did the colour start?
[SEG0009] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm I can't pin the day. I properly saw it yesterday, but it might've been coming before that. I really don't know the start.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? An email just jumped over the notes.
[SEG0011] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah I can't tell you when it started. Noticed it properly yesterday. Anything before that I'm guessing.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ok. Tell me about the feeds.
[SEG0013] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Breast milk, and we top up with formula, the Aptamil, roughly every four hours. He'll do a good twenty minutes then the bottle if he's still rooting.
[SEG0014] person_4 (PATIENT): Mmm.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Every four hours, breast plus formula. Any vomiting?
[SEG0016] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. No spews at all.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0018] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. He feels warm sometimes but not hot, not feverish.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the nappies? Any pale poos, or dark wee?
[SEG0020] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Wee's yellow, not dark, plenty of wet nappies. Poos are that mustard colour, not pale.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is he hard to wake, floppy, that sort of thing?
[SEG0022] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Nah he wakes himself for the feeds, cranky till he's on, then he's out. Not floppy.
[SEG0023] person_4 (PATIENT): Wah.

[SEG0024] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I know, I know, shh. Random, but my sister's been on biotin, she says bioten, for her hair, and she keeps telling me to give it to the bub, which I have not done. And my husband takes metforman for his diabetes. Nothing to do with Arlo, sorry, I go off.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hang on, the screen refreshed. Your husband is on what?
[SEG0026] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Metforman, for his diabetes. Not the baby. Arlo's on no medicines at all.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies for him? Medicines, milk, anything?
[SEG0028] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, nothing like that.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look. Pop him on the cot if you can.
[SEG0030] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He hates being unwrapped, just so you know. We had a shocking night too, the neighbour's dog went off at about two.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sclera are yellow, and the skin's yellow down to about the nipple line. Fontanelle's soft, not sunken. Belly's soft, and he looks well hydrated.
[SEG0032] person_4 (PATIENT): Eh.

[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): So, day ten, yellow to the chest, feeding every four hours, weight up on birth, and I'm turning over ordinary physiological jaundice, breast milk jaundice, not enough intake, with haemolysis further down if there was a blood group issue. I am not going to conclude this is liver disease. My leaning is physiological jaundice, and I can't rule out breast milk jaundice. Let's see what the tests say before I go any further.

[SEG0034] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Is breast milk jaundice a bad one? My cousin stopped breastfeeding over something and I really don't want to, the lactation lady was lovely but hospital parking is a joke.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not stopping the breast milk today. Sorry, the feed interval, say it once more?
[SEG0036] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Every four hours. Breast, then a formula top up.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. We'll do a bilirubin blood test today, before you leave. And I'll book a repeat bilirubin for Thursday morning. No need to fast him.
[SEG0038] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I can take today's one in the treatment room in a few minutes. Thursday I've got half eight.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. If Thursday's result is borderline we'll do a third blood test. If the yellow does not settle, we'll organise an abdominal ultrasound.
[SEG0040] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A scan, is that like urgent? My head goes straight to the worst thing.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Only if it doesn't settle. Not booked now. I'll see you back in two weeks with the numbers either way.
[SEG0042] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Two weeks, yep. Do I keep the formula top ups or is that making it worse?

[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep the breastfeeding and the formula top ups as you are. Wake him if he stretches past four hours. If he becomes hard to wake or the yellow spreads to his legs, bring him straight in.
[SEG0044] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hard to wake, or yellow down the legs. Got it. My husband'll panic, he panicked when his own sugar was up before the metforman.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): His diabetes isn't Arlo's problem. Questions about the blood test?
[SEG0046] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Will it hurt, he's so tiny. And I left the dummy in the car, typical me.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): It's a heel prick, quick, he'll grizzle. You can feed him straight after.
[SEG0048] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ok. Thursday half eight, no fasting, I'll set an alarm. The pram better behave.
[SEG0049] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Thursday at half eight, no fast. I'll write it on the card so it doesn't get lost.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): And just so it's clear, if those Thursday numbers are borderline we do the third test, and the scan only if the colour hangs around. No medicine from me today.
[SEG0051] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thank goodness. I can't keep names straight, bioten, metforman, whatever my sister's into this month.
[SEG0052] person_4 (PATIENT): Mmm mm.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll leave it there. Nurse'll take you for the heel prick, and I'll see you in two weeks.
[SEG0054] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Come on Arlo. He won't say thanks but I will. Thanks, both of you.

spec.situation: Parents with a ten-day-old baby, yellow skin and feeding every four hours; weight read by the nurse; breast milk plus formula; blood test for bilirubin planned today.

traps.happens: In the plan the doctor books some tests or visits for a definite time ('the nurse takes bloods Thursday morning', 'I'll see you in two weeks') and makes others conditional ('if those are borderline we do the third test', 'if it does not settle, a scan').
traps.label_rule: Booked or arranged = status planned. Only the hedged ones are conditional. Never mark a booked test conditional or 'if needed'. Instructions for the booked test (fasting, time, medicine timing) belong to that test's action, not a separate invented plan item.

features: doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats
